screens.title: Interfacing Switches and LEDs
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn how switches and LEDs connect to a microcontroller in a way that is predictable, safe, and easy to debug. We start with the practical problem: a switch contact that is not pressed leaves a pin floating and susceptible to noise, which you fix with pull-up or pull-down resistors. You'll see how the TM4C123G provides internal pull resistors you can enable in software, and when you should use external resistors on a breadboard. We'll also cover switch bounce: why a single mechanical press can look like many transitions, and two simple software patterns to debounce reliably. Finally, you will practice wiring LEDs with a 220 ohm current-limiting resistor and understand why driving directly without one risks the GPIO pin. By the end of the module you can wire two switches and two LEDs on a breadboard, enable internal pull-ups for the LaunchPad switches, and implement debouncing in your program. Think about a concrete outcome: your board will toggle LEDs predictably when you press a switch, with no ghost presses and no damaged pins.

screens.title: Floating Inputs and Defined States
screens.narratorSegment: A floating input is a GPIO pin that is not tied to a voltage source when the switch is open, and that lack of a defined connection lets electrical noise drive the reading to HIGH or LOW unpredictably. In practice, a student will wire a switch so that when it is not pressed the pin is disconnected; without a pull resistor the microcontroller can sample random voltages and produce spurious events. A pull-up resistor connects the pin weakly to the positive supply, so the idle reading is HIGH and only drops to LOW when the switch closes to ground. Conversely, a pull-down resistor ties the pin to ground so the idle reading is LOW and becomes HIGH when the switch connects it to supply. A simple concrete example: on the LaunchPad the built-in switches are active-low with internal pull-ups enabled, so the pin reads HIGH at rest and reads LOW when you press the switch. A common misconception is that the internal pull-up is a strong connection; it is intentionally weak so it doesn't source large currents, which is why we pick values like 10 kiloohm externally when needed. Key takeaway: always ensure every input has a defined idle state with a pull-up or pull-down to avoid ghost triggers. Which idle state fits your switch wiring and system logic?

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Floating Inputs and Defined States
Floating Inputs and Defined States
Why pull resistors prevent random readings
Definition
A floating input is not connected to supply or ground when the switch is open. It may pick up interference and change state without a physical press. Pull-up and pull-down resistors provide a weak connection so the pin has a deterministic idle voltage.
Key points
  • Pull-up ties pin to 3.3 volts through a resistor; idle reading is HIGH.
  • Pull-down ties pin to ground; idle reading is LOW.
  • Use 10 kΩ as a common external value when internal resistors are unsuitable.
Concrete example
LaunchPad built-in switches are active-low with pull-ups. When not pressed the pin reads HIGH; pressing connects to ground and the pin reads LOW.
Analogy
Think of a pull-up like a gentle spring that holds the pin up unless you press it down to ground.
Common mistake
Assuming an unconnected pin will remain stable. Without a resistor, readings can flip randomly and cause false interrupts or toggles.
Key Takeaway
Always give each input a defined idle level using pull-ups or pull-downs to prevent random behavior.

screens.title: Pull-Up vs Pull-Down Resistors
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between a pull-up and a pull-down resistor depends on how you wire the switch and what idle signal you prefer. A pull-up sets the idle reading to HIGH and requires the switch to connect the pin to ground to produce LOW; this is the pattern used by the LaunchPad's built-in switches, which are active-low. A pull-down sets the idle to LOW and makes pressing the switch drive the pin HIGH. A practical reason to prefer pull-ups is that many development boards expect active-low switches and have internal pull-ups available. On the other hand, a pull-down may be clearer if your external circuitry sources a signal when pressed. For a concrete example, wiring an external switch to Port E pin 0 with a 10 kiloohm pull-down makes the pin read LOW until the switch connects it to 3.3 volts. A common misconception is that one choice is always safer; instead think about noise sources and how you want peripherals to respond during resets. Use external resistors when you need a specific resistor value, or when internal pull resistors are not present or adequate. Closing question: which idle state reduces risk in your particular circuit and why?

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Pull-Up vs Pull-Down Resistors
Pull-Up vs Pull-Down
Compare when to use each and why
Pull-Up
Idle = HIGH. Switch connects pin to ground when pressed. Common on LaunchPad built-in switches. Internal pull-up can be enabled in software.
Example: PF4 reads HIGH at rest; press the active-low switch and it reads LOW.
When to use
When board design or signal convention expects active-low inputs, or when you want defined HIGH idle.
Pull-Down
Idle = LOW. Switch connects pin to supply when pressed. Use when external circuitry naturally sources the signal or when active-high makes logic clearer.
Example: External switch on Port E pin 0 with 10 kiloohm pull-down reads LOW until pressed, then HIGH.
When to use
When you need a LOW default or when your wiring sources voltage on press.
Common misconception
Thinking internal pull-ups are strong enough for every case. Use external resistors when you need a precise value or stronger noise immunity.
Key Takeaway
Pick pull-up or pull-down to match your switch wiring and board conventions; use external resistors when you need control over the resistor value.

screens.title: Enabling Internal Pull-Ups on the TM4C123G
screens.narratorSegment: The TM4C123G provides per-pin internal pull-up and pull-down resistors controlled by dedicated registers. The names to remember are GPIOPUR for pull-ups and GPIOPDR for pull-downs. To enable a pull-up on Port F bits zero and four, you set the corresponding bits in the GPIOPUR register. The chapter gives a concrete C example that writes to the memory-mapped register address for GPIO_PORTF_PUR_R and sets bits for PF0 and PF4. Conceptually, that single write tells the hardware to weakly connect those pins to 3.3 volts when no other connection drives them. Use this when you prefer not to place external resistors on the breadboard. A common pitfall is assuming that enabling an internal pull-up changes drive strength or direction; it does not make the pin an output nor does it change how much current the pin can source when driven. Another practical check: after enabling the pull-up, confirm the pin reads the expected idle level before attaching interrupts or toggling outputs. Try enabling and then reading the data register to see the stable value. Takeaway: internal pull resistors are convenient for quick prototypes, but verify behavior with a meter or test code before relying on them.

keyIdea.title: Registers to know
keyIdea.text: GPIOPUR enables pull-up, GPIOPDR enables pull-down. Set the specific bits for the pins you want to affect.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Enabling Internal Pull-Ups
Enabling Internal Pull-Ups
GPIOPUR and GPIOPDR control internal pull resistors
Code example (visual)
// Memory-mapped register alias
#define GPIO_PORTF_PUR_R    (*((volatile uint32_t *)0x40025510))

// Enable pull-up for PF0 and PF4
GPIO_PORTF_PUR_R |= 0x11;  // Bits 0 and 4
This write sets the pull-up bit for each pin. After this, the hardware provides a weak connection to 3.3 volts when the pin is not driven.
Quick checklist
  • Enable clock to the port before touching registers.
  • Set the pull-up bit in GPIOPUR for the specific pins.
  • Confirm the pin reads the expected idle value after enabling.
Misconception
Enabling a pull-up is not the same as configuring the pin as an output. It only affects the internal resistor when the pin is an input.

screens.title: External Resistors and Breadboard Wiring
screens.narratorSegment: Using external resistors on a breadboard gives you control over exact values and improves noise immunity. The typical choices from the chapter are 10 kiloohm for pull-up or pull-down resistors and 220 ohm for LED current limiting with a 3.3 volt GPIO. To wire an external pull-up: connect one side of the 10 kiloohm resistor to 3.3 volts and the other side to the input pin; place the switch between the pin and ground. For a pull-down, connect the resistor between the pin and ground and wire the switch to 3.3 volts. For LEDs, always put a 220 ohm resistor in series with the anode. The longer leg (anode) goes to the resistor then to the GPIO pin; the shorter leg (cathode) goes to ground. A common student error is placing the resistor in parallel instead of series with the LED or forgetting to connect the GPIO pin to the resistor. In your hands-on build you'll wire two external switches and two external LEDs: one switch uses an internal pull-up on PF0, the other uses an external 10 kiloohm pull-down on PE0; LEDs connect to Port B pins with 220 ohm resistors. Quick sanity check: measure continuity and look for obvious shorts before powering the board. How will you verify each LED lights only when its GPIO is driven HIGH?

keyIdea.text: 10k for pull resistors, 220Ω series resistor for LEDs. Resistors for LEDs must be in series with the anode to limit current.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › External Resistors and Breadboard Wiring
Breadboard Wiring Patterns
Place pull resistors and LED resistors correctly to avoid floating pins and overcurrent.
Pull resistor wiring
  1. For pull-up: resistor between 3.3V rail and the input pin; switch between pin and ground.
  2. For pull-down: resistor between pin and ground; switch between pin and 3.3V.
  3. Use 10 kΩ for most cases; stronger pull means less noise but more idle current.
LED wiring
Connect GPIO → 220 Ω resistor → LED anode (long leg); LED cathode (short leg) → ground. When the pin is driven HIGH the LED lights; when LOW it is off.
Pro tip
Label wires and resistor values on your breadboard so you don't confuse pull resistors with LED resistors during debugging.
Example build
One switch on PF0 with internal pull-up enabled; one switch on PE0 with external 10 kΩ pull-down. LEDs on PB0 and PB1 each with 220 Ω in series. This mirrors the hands-on activity in the chapter.

screens.title: Active-Low Switches and RGB LED Pins
screens.narratorSegment: The LaunchPad exposes two user switches on Port F pins zero and four and an RGB LED wired to pins one, two, and three. Importantly, the user switches are active-low: they pull the pin to ground when pressed and rely on pull-up resistors to read HIGH at rest. Knowing this convention prevents logic mistakes like toggling the LED on when you mean to turn it off. For the RGB LED, each color channel connects to a separate pin, so you can create colors by setting individual pins HIGH or LOW depending on the LED wiring. Always remember to include a resistor in series with each LED channel if you wire external single-color LEDs; the board's on-board RGB connection is already designed for the LaunchPad but external LEDs require the 220 ohm resistor rule. A common student error is treating the built-in switches as active-high and inverting the logic incorrectly in software. Test: read the pin while leaving the switch alone and while pressing it; you should see HIGH then LOW for an active-low switch. Final takeaway: match your software logic to the hardware's active level to avoid inverted behavior.

keyIdea.text: LaunchPad switches are active-low; RGB channels are separate pins—treat each LED channel as an independent GPIO output with current limiting.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Active-Low Switches and RGB Pins
Active-Low Switches & RGB Pins
Match software logic to hardware active levels
Switches
SW1 and SW2 connect to PF0 and PF4 and are active-low. The board enables internal pull-ups so the pin reads HIGH when untouched and LOW when pressed.
Quick check: read the pin at rest and while pressing to confirm the expected HIGH then LOW pattern.
RGB LED
The RGB LED maps three channels to pins 1, 2, and 3. Driving each channel individually lets you mix colors; for external LEDs always include a 220 Ω resistor.
Key Takeaway
Confirm active level before writing logic: an active-low switch inverts the natural meaning of a HIGH/LOW read for your code.

screens.title: Switch Bounce Over Time
screens.narratorSegment: When a mechanical switch closes, the metal contacts do not make a perfect single transition. Instead, they physically bounce against each other for a few milliseconds, causing the voltage at the pin to fluctuate between HIGH and LOW several times. This physical bounce can easily produce tens or hundreds of micro-transitions depending on the switch. The lesson shows a simple timeline: initial contact, rapid bounce oscillations, and final steady contact. Practically, this means a single human press could look like several presses to a program that samples quickly. To handle this, software debouncing waits for the signal to become stable for a short window before accepting the change. A common mistake is relying on hardware sampling alone; if your loop or interrupt fires faster than the bounce settles, you'll see multiple events. Example: if you sample a switch in a tight loop without debounce and increment a counter on each detected press, a single press could increment the counter many times. Takeaway: treat switch inputs as noisy for a short time after a transition and only accept changes that remain stable for the debounce interval.

keyIdea.text: Mechanical switches bounce for a few milliseconds; wait for stability or use a debounce algorithm to avoid multiple detections.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Switch Bounce Over Time
Switch Bounce Over Time
A simple timeline shows initial contact, bouncing, then steady contact
Phase 1
Initial contact: the switch first touches and may briefly close the circuit.
Phase 2
Bounce: contacts oscillate for a few milliseconds causing multiple HIGH/LOW transitions.
Phase 3
Steady: contacts settle and the pin remains in the pressed state until release.
Practical example
If your code samples faster than the bounce interval, each oscillation may trigger your press detection. Debounce by waiting a short interval for the signal to remain stable.
Key Takeaway
Treat switches as noisy for a few milliseconds after transitions and verify stability before acting.

screens.title: Debouncing with a Stability Counter
screens.narratorSegment: A commonly used debouncing approach is to track the last reading and increment a counter when the current reading equals the last. If the reading changes, reset the counter. Only when the counter exceeds a chosen threshold do we accept the new reading as stable. The chapter provides an example that reads PF4 and uses a debounceCounter variable that increments each time the reading matches the last recorded state; when the counter grows past a threshold the function returns the stable value. This method is robust because it requires multiple consecutive samples, reducing sensitivity to brief bounces. A concrete example: if your loop samples every hundred microseconds and you require 10000 stable increments as in the chapter, you create a stable window long enough to filter the bounce. A misconception to avoid is choosing thresholds arbitrarily large so your interface feels unresponsive. Tune the threshold to the switch characteristics and how responsive you want the UI. Finally, remember to check for state changes to toggle LEDs or generate events only when the debounced value actually changes. How will you choose sample rate and threshold to balance responsiveness and reliability?

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Debouncing with a Stability Counter
Debounce: Stability Counter
Require consecutive stable reads before accepting the change
Code pattern (visual)
uint32_t lastState = 0;
uint32_t debounceCounter = 0;

uint32_t debouncedRead(void) {
    uint32_t currentState = GPIO_PORTF_DATA_R & 0x10;  // Read PF4

    if (currentState != lastState) {
        debounceCounter = 0;
        lastState = currentState;
    } else {
        debounceCounter++;
        if (debounceCounter > 10000) {
            return currentState;
        }
    }
    return lastState;  // Return stable state
}
This function only returns a new value after the counter indicates stability. Adjust the threshold to fit your timing and responsiveness needs.
Pros
Very robust against short bounces; works well when loop timing is consistent.
Caution
Picking an overly large threshold causes sluggish response. Measure typical bounce duration to set a reasonable threshold.
Key Takeaway
Use consecutive stable samples to confirm a switch state before acting; tune the threshold for responsiveness.

screens.title: Simple Double-Read Debounce
screens.narratorSegment: A simpler debounce approach shown in the chapter is the double-read pattern: read the switch, wait for a short, fixed delay, then read it again. If the two reads match, accept the result; if not, assume bouncing and treat the input as unchanged or retry. This method is easy to implement and works well when you only need a lightweight filter and can tolerate a fixed delay. The example uses a delay loop and compares two readings of PF4 separated by a small wait. The tradeoff is responsiveness: the fixed delay adds latency to every acknowledged transition, so you should pick a delay long enough to outlast the bounce but short enough to preserve user experience. A common mistake is using too short a delay which won't filter bounce, or too long a delay that makes the interface feel sluggish. For a concrete scenario, a 5 to 20 millisecond delay often suffices for ordinary switches; measure your hardware if you need tighter bounds. Final question: in your project, do you prefer the simplicity of double-read or the precision of a counter-based approach?

Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Simple Double-Read Debounce
Double-Read Debounce
A straightforward method that balances simplicity and effectiveness
Code pattern (visual)
uint32_t readSwitch(void) {
    uint32_t first = GPIO_PORTF_DATA_R & 0x10;
    delay(10000);  // Wait for bounce to settle
    uint32_t second = GPIO_PORTF_DATA_R & 0x10;
    if (first == second) {
        return second;
    }
    return 0x10;  // Not pressed if bouncing
}
If the two readings match, the switch is accepted. The delay value should be chosen based on typical bounce duration.
Pros
Very simple to implement and reason about; useful for quick prototypes.
Tradeoff
Adds a fixed delay per check which can make the interface feel slower if the delay is long.
Key Takeaway
Use double-read for simplicity, and tune delay to be long enough to outlast bounce but short enough to stay responsive.

screens.title: Build: Two Switches and Two LEDs
screens.narratorSegment: The hands-on activity ties together wiring and software. On the breadboard, place two switches and two LEDs. Connect one switch to Port F pin zero and enable the internal pull-up in software; this switch will be active-low. screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
screens.narratorSegment: Students often make a few recurring mistakes that are easy to diagnose and fix. The first is connecting a switch directly to a GPIO without any pull resistor. In that case the pin floats when the switch is open, producing random readings; the fix is to add a pull-up or pull-down resistor or enable the internal pull-up. Second, placing the LED resistor in parallel instead of in series means the LED may draw too much current and the resistor does not limit it; always place the resistor between the GPIO and LED anode. Third, misunderstanding active-low switches leads to inverted software logic—test the idle and pressed readings before coding. A practical assessment from the chapter is to show a diagram of a switch with no resistor and ask what is wrong and how to fix it. For each common mistake, the remedy is straightforward: add the missing resistor, correct resistor placement, or flip the logic in code after confirming the electrical behavior. As a debugging mindset, measure idle voltages and watch the pin readings while you press the switch to observe the real behavior before changing the software.

Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
Practical fixes for frequent wiring and code errors
Mistake
No pull resistor on a switch (floating input).
Fix: add a pull-up or pull-down, or enable internal pull-up.
Mistake
Resistor placed in parallel with LED instead of series.
Fix: move resistor between GPIO and LED anode so it limits current.
Mistake
Assuming switches are active-high when they are active-low.
Fix: observe pin at rest and on press, then implement logic accordingly.

screens.title: GPIO Current Limits and Safe LED Driving
screens.narratorSegment: Microcontroller GPIO pins can source or sink only limited current. The chapter emphasizes using a 220 ohm resistor when driving LEDs from a 3.3 volt GPIO to keep current at safe levels for the pin and the LED. The resistor value follows Ohm's law: it reduces current when the pin outputs HIGH so the LED draws a manageable amount. In practice, that means connect GPIO to resistor to LED anode, and LED cathode to ground. Do not tie many LEDs directly to a single pin or expect a pin to drive motors or high-current loads. If you need higher current, use a transistor or driver stage. Another important safety check is to verify wiring before powering the board; a short to ground or to Vcc can immediately exceed safe currents. A common mistake is omitting the LED resistor because the LED appears to light briefly; this can damage the pin over time. Final reflection: always design outputs with current limits in mind and choose external drivers when you need more than a single pin can safely provide. GPIO Current Limits and Safe LED Driving means use a 220 ω resistor for leds on 3.3v gpios and avoid driving high-current loads directly from a pin.. In practical terms, protect pins by limiting led current and avoiding excessive source/sink loads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

GPIO Current Limits and Safe LED Driving
Always limit current to protect the MCU and LEDs
LED wiring rule
Use GPIO → 220 Ω → LED anode → LED cathode → ground. The resistor limits current so the pin and LED are not damaged.
When to use drivers
If you need to drive more current than a pin allows, switch to a transistor or dedicated LED driver rather than paralleling many LEDs on a single pin.
Common mistake
Omitting the resistor because the LED lights briefly—this damages the pin over time. Always include a series resistor and verify with a meter before long-term use.

Respect GPIO current limits. Use a 220 Ω resistor for 3.3V LEDs and add a transistor driver for higher loads.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essentials. First, floating inputs are unreliable; always give an input a defined idle state using a pull-up or pull-down resistor. Second, the TM4C123G provides internal pull-up and pull-down registers—GPIOPUR and GPIOPDR—that let you enable weak pulls in software, which is convenient for quick prototypes. Third, external resistors are still important: use 10 kiloohm for pull resistors on the breadboard when you need a specific value or stronger behavior. Fourth, mechanical switches bounce; use software debouncing patterns such as a stability counter or a double-read with delay to filter spurious transitions. Finally, always protect outputs with a series resistor—220 ohm is a common choice for LEDs on a 3.3 volt GPIO—and avoid driving high-current loads from a single pin. Keep these concepts in mind when you wire and code: defined idle states, reliable debouncing, and safe output current form the foundation of predictable embedded input/output.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how switches and LEDs connect to a microcontroller in a way that is predictable, safe, and easy to debug. We start with the practical problem: a switch contact that is not pressed leaves a pin floating and susceptible to noise, which you fix with pull-up or pull-down resistors. You'll see how the TM4C123G provides internal pull resistors you can enable in software, and when you should use external resistors on a breadboard. We'll also cover switch bounce: why a single mechanical press can look like many transitions, and two simple software patterns to debounce reliably. Finally, you will practice wiring LEDs with a 220 ohm current-limiting resistor and understand why driving directly without one risks the GPIO pin. By the end of the module you can wire two switches and two LEDs on a breadboard, enable internal pull-ups for the LaunchPad switches, and implement debouncing in your program. Think about a concrete outcome: your board will toggle LEDs predictably when you press a switch, with no ghost presses and no damaged pins.

These objectives focus on practical wiring and reliable software. First, you'll connect external switches and LEDs to the LaunchPad and verify they work using a breadboard. That means correct pin selection, resistor placement, and simple validation tests. Second, you'll explain and apply pull-up and pull-down resistors. You'll be able to describe why floating inputs are dangerous and choose an internal or external resistor as appropriate. Third, you'll enable and use the TM4C123G internal pull-up or pull-down registers, knowing which register controls the hardware behavior. Finally, you'll implement software debouncing to eliminate false triggers from mechanical switch bounce. Each objective pairs a hands-on task with a conceptual check so you can both perform the wiring and explain why it prevents noise or damage. By the end you will show a working breadboard where pressing a switch toggles an LED without ghost events.

Beyond wiring and code, these objectives stress inspection and explanation. You should be able to point to a floating input and say why it can produce random HIGH or LOW readings. You'll demonstrate enabling GPIOPUR bits for the TM4C123G and explain why that sets a pin's idle level without external hardware. You'll pick appropriate resistor values—10 kiloohm for pull-ups or pull-downs on a breadboard and 220 ohm for LED current limiting—and justify those choices from the perspective of protecting the pin and preserving signal integrity. Finally, you'll debug a bouncing switch by using the two simple debounce approaches presented in the lesson and explain the tradeoffs: one is quick to write and coarse, the other can be more precise. These checks help you move from following steps to understanding why each step matters in embedded projects.

A floating input is a GPIO pin that is not tied to a voltage source when the switch is open, and that lack of a defined connection lets electrical noise drive the reading to HIGH or LOW unpredictably. In practice, a student will wire a switch so that when it is not pressed the pin is disconnected; without a pull resistor the microcontroller can sample random voltages and produce spurious events. A pull-up resistor connects the pin weakly to the positive supply, so the idle reading is HIGH and only drops to LOW when the switch closes to ground. Conversely, a pull-down resistor ties the pin to ground so the idle reading is LOW and becomes HIGH when the switch connects it to supply. A simple concrete example: on the LaunchPad the built-in switches are active-low with internal pull-ups enabled, so the pin reads HIGH at rest and reads LOW when you press the switch. A common misconception is that the internal pull-up is a strong connection; it is intentionally weak so it doesn't source large currents, which is why we pick values like 10 kiloohm externally when needed. Key takeaway: always ensure every input has a defined idle state with a pull-up or pull-down to avoid ghost triggers. Which idle state fits your switch wiring and system logic?

Choosing between a pull-up and a pull-down resistor depends on how you wire the switch and what idle signal you prefer. A pull-up sets the idle reading to HIGH and requires the switch to connect the pin to ground to produce LOW; this is the pattern used by the LaunchPad's built-in switches, which are active-low. A pull-down sets the idle to LOW and makes pressing the switch drive the pin HIGH. A practical reason to prefer pull-ups is that many development boards expect active-low switches and have internal pull-ups available. On the other hand, a pull-down may be clearer if your external circuitry sources a signal when pressed. For a concrete example, wiring an external switch to Port E pin 0 with a 10 kiloohm pull-down makes the pin read LOW until the switch connects it to 3.3 volts. A common misconception is that one choice is always safer; instead think about noise sources and how you want peripherals to respond during resets. Use external resistors when you need a specific resistor value, or when internal pull resistors are not present or adequate. Closing question: which idle state reduces risk in your particular circuit and why?

The TM4C123G provides per-pin internal pull-up and pull-down resistors controlled by dedicated registers. The names to remember are GPIOPUR for pull-ups and GPIOPDR for pull-downs. To enable a pull-up on Port F bits zero and four, you set the corresponding bits in the GPIOPUR register. The chapter gives a concrete C example that writes to the memory-mapped register address for GPIO_PORTF_PUR_R and sets bits for PF0 and PF4. Conceptually, that single write tells the hardware to weakly connect those pins to 3.3 volts when no other connection drives them. Use this when you prefer not to place external resistors on the breadboard. A common pitfall is assuming that enabling an internal pull-up changes drive strength or direction; it does not make the pin an output nor does it change how much current the pin can source when driven. Another practical check: after enabling the pull-up, confirm the pin reads the expected idle level before attaching interrupts or toggling outputs. Try enabling and then reading the data register to see the stable value. Takeaway: internal pull resistors are convenient for quick prototypes, but verify behavior with a meter or test code before relying on them.

Using external resistors on a breadboard gives you control over exact values and improves noise immunity. The typical choices from the chapter are 10 kiloohm for pull-up or pull-down resistors and 220 ohm for LED current limiting with a 3.3 volt GPIO. To wire an external pull-up: connect one side of the 10 kiloohm resistor to 3.3 volts and the other side to the input pin; place the switch between the pin and ground. For a pull-down, connect the resistor between the pin and ground and wire the switch to 3.3 volts. For LEDs, always put a 220 ohm resistor in series with the anode. The longer leg (anode) goes to the resistor then to the GPIO pin; the shorter leg (cathode) goes to ground. A common student error is placing the resistor in parallel instead of series with the LED or forgetting to connect the GPIO pin to the resistor. In your hands-on build you'll wire two external switches and two external LEDs: one switch uses an internal pull-up on PF0, the other uses an external 10 kiloohm pull-down on PE0; LEDs connect to Port B pins with 220 ohm resistors. Quick sanity check: measure continuity and look for obvious shorts before powering the board. How will you verify each LED lights only when its GPIO is driven HIGH?

The LaunchPad exposes two user switches on Port F pins zero and four and an RGB LED wired to pins one, two, and three. Importantly, the user switches are active-low: they pull the pin to ground when pressed and rely on pull-up resistors to read HIGH at rest. Knowing this convention prevents logic mistakes like toggling the LED on when you mean to turn it off. For the RGB LED, each color channel connects to a separate pin, so you can create colors by setting individual pins HIGH or LOW depending on the LED wiring. Always remember to include a resistor in series with each LED channel if you wire external single-color LEDs; the board's on-board RGB connection is already designed for the LaunchPad but external LEDs require the 220 ohm resistor rule. A common student error is treating the built-in switches as active-high and inverting the logic incorrectly in software. Test: read the pin while leaving the switch alone and while pressing it; you should see HIGH then LOW for an active-low switch. Final takeaway: match your software logic to the hardware's active level to avoid inverted behavior.

When a mechanical switch closes, the metal contacts do not make a perfect single transition. Instead, they physically bounce against each other for a few milliseconds, causing the voltage at the pin to fluctuate between HIGH and LOW several times. This physical bounce can easily produce tens or hundreds of micro-transitions depending on the switch. The lesson shows a simple timeline: initial contact, rapid bounce oscillations, and final steady contact. Practically, this means a single human press could look like several presses to a program that samples quickly. To handle this, software debouncing waits for the signal to become stable for a short window before accepting the change. A common mistake is relying on hardware sampling alone; if your loop or interrupt fires faster than the bounce settles, you'll see multiple events. Example: if you sample a switch in a tight loop without debounce and increment a counter on each detected press, a single press could increment the counter many times. Takeaway: treat switch inputs as noisy for a short time after a transition and only accept changes that remain stable for the debounce interval.

A commonly used debouncing approach is to track the last reading and increment a counter when the current reading equals the last. If the reading changes, reset the counter. Only when the counter exceeds a chosen threshold do we accept the new reading as stable. The chapter provides an example that reads PF4 and uses a debounceCounter variable that increments each time the reading matches the last recorded state; when the counter grows past a threshold the function returns the stable value. This method is robust because it requires multiple consecutive samples, reducing sensitivity to brief bounces. A concrete example: if your loop samples every hundred microseconds and you require 10000 stable increments as in the chapter, you create a stable window long enough to filter the bounce. A misconception to avoid is choosing thresholds arbitrarily large so your interface feels unresponsive. Tune the threshold to the switch characteristics and how responsive you want the UI. Finally, remember to check for state changes to toggle LEDs or generate events only when the debounced value actually changes. How will you choose sample rate and threshold to balance responsiveness and reliability?

A simpler debounce approach shown in the chapter is the double-read pattern: read the switch, wait for a short, fixed delay, then read it again. If the two reads match, accept the result; if not, assume bouncing and treat the input as unchanged or retry. This method is easy to implement and works well when you only need a lightweight filter and can tolerate a fixed delay. The example uses a delay loop and compares two readings of PF4 separated by a small wait. The tradeoff is responsiveness: the fixed delay adds latency to every acknowledged transition, so you should pick a delay long enough to outlast the bounce but short enough to preserve user experience. A common mistake is using too short a delay which won't filter bounce, or too long a delay that makes the interface feel sluggish. For a concrete scenario, a 5 to 20 millisecond delay often suffices for ordinary switches; measure your hardware if you need tighter bounds. Final question: in your project, do you prefer the simplicity of double-read or the precision of a counter-based approach?
